entities.summary:
Manuel Antonio Flórez Maldonado Martínez Ángulo y Bodquín (1723–1799) emerged as a formidable figure in the late 18th-century Spanish Empire, serving as a general in the Spanish navy and, critically, as viceroy of both New Granada (1776–1782) and New Spain (1787–1789). His tenure coincided with an era of intense Bourbon administrative reform and escalating imperial competition, particularly with Great Britain, positioning him at the forefront of efforts to consolidate Spanish power and rationalize colonial governance across vast American territories.

Flórez's administrative career began in earnest with his appointment as Viceroy of New Granada in 1776, where he faced the formidable challenge of the Comuneros Revolt of 1781. This widespread popular uprising, sparked by increased taxation and monopolistic policies, was ultimately suppressed under his command, albeit through a combination of military force and strategic concessions. He also dedicated significant resources to fortifying strategic Caribbean ports, notably Cartagena de Indias, against potential British attacks during the American Revolutionary War, demonstrating his naval background and strategic foresight. Following his successful, if tumultuous, term in New Granada, he was transferred to the prestigious Viceroyalty of New Spain in 1787, where he focused on economic reforms, particularly enhancing the tobacco monopoly and boosting silver mining output.
